meta.title: Who really said "In this theater of man's life it is reserved only for God and angels to be lookers on"? | Quotle.info
meta.description: Not Pythagoras. Francis Bacon wrote it in The Advancement of Learning (1605), and he was arguing against Pythagoras's praise of the onlooker.
meta.ogTitle: Who really said 'In this theater of man's life it is reserved only for God and angels to be lookers on'?
meta.ogDescription: Francis Bacon, The Advancement of Learning (1605), Book II. The line answers Pythagoras rather than quoting him: only God and angels may simply watch.

answer.label: Not Pythagoras — actually Francis Bacon
answer.sourceLine: Bacon wrote it in The Advancement of Learning (1605), Book II, xx, 8. He first retells Pythagoras’s comparison of life to the Olympic games, where the onlookers are the best class of people. Then he turns it around: “But men must know, that in this theatre of man’s life it is reserved only for God and angels to be lookers on.” The line is a rebuttal of Pythagoras, not a saying of his.

source.heading: Where it comes from
source.excerpt: For first, it decideth the question touching the preferment of the contemplative or active life, and decideth it against Aristotle. … not much unlike to that comparison which Pythagoras made for the gracing and magnifying of philosophy and contemplation, who being asked what he was, answered, “That if Hiero were ever at the Olympian games, he knew the manner, that some came to try their fortune for the prizes, and some came as merchants to utter their commodities, and some came to make good cheer and meet their friends, and some came to look on; and that he was one of them that came to look on.” But men must know, that in this theatre of man’s life it is reserved only for God and angels to be lookers on.
trail: The sentence appears word for word in Bacon’s The Advancement of Learning, Book II, chapter XX, section (8), right after Bacon retells Pythagoras’s Olympic-games comparison: Project Gutenberg text ↗.
Wikiquote’s Pythagoras page lists the line under “Misattributed” and credits it to Francis Bacon, The Advancement of Learning (1605), Book II, xx, 8: Wikiquote: Pythagoras ↗.
Wikiquote’s Francis Bacon page gives the full sentence (“But men must know that…”) among its Advancement of Learning quotations, cited to Book II, xx, 8: Wikiquote: Francis Bacon ↗.

The idea Bacon is answering really is attributed to Pythagoras. In Cicero’s Tusculan Disputations, Book V, Pythagoras says the spectators at the games were “by far the best”: C. D. Yonge translation, Project Gutenberg ↗.
source.excerptNote: The text follows Henry Morley’s edition with modernized spelling, as transcribed by Project Gutenberg from the 1893 Cassell & Company printing. The popular version drops “But men must know, that,” uses the American spelling “theater,” and so hides that Bacon is disagreeing with Pythagoras.

author.name: Francis Bacon
author.heading: Who wrote it
author.bio: Francis Bacon was an English philosopher and statesman who served as Attorney General and Lord Chancellor of England under King James I. He argued for natural philosophy guided by the scientific method. The Advancement of Learning (1605), his survey of human knowledge written in English, contains this line.

copyAttribution: “But men must know, that in this theatre of man’s life it is reserved only for God and angels to be lookers on.” — Francis Bacon, The Advancement of Learning (1605), Book II, xx, 8. Often misattributed to Pythagoras.

misattribution.heading: Why it gets pinned on Pythagoras
misattribution.intro: The sentence follows straight on from Bacon’s retelling of a famous Pythagoras story. Lifted out of the paragraph, it is easy to credit to the man named just before it.

items.why: Wikiquote’s Pythagoras page files this exact wording under “Misattributed” and gives the true source as Francis Bacon, The Advancement of Learning (1605), Book II, xx, 8 (Wikiquote ↗). Pythagoras’s actual view, as Cicero reports it, was the opposite: the onlookers at the games were “by far the best” (Tusculan Disputations, Book V ↗).

misattribution.truthLine: Francis Bacon wrote it in The Advancement of Learning (1605), Book II, xx, 8, to reject Pythagoras’s praise of the onlooker (full text ↗).

context.heading: What Bacon meant
lead: Bacon was weighing the contemplative life against the active life, and he decided the question “against Aristotle.” He compared Aristotle’s reasons for contemplation to Pythagoras’s famous answer when asked what he was. People come to the Olympic games to compete, to trade or to meet friends, and some come only to watch; Pythagoras counted himself among the watchers.

Bacon’s reply is the line now credited to Pythagoras. Human life is a stage where everyone has a part, and only God and the angels may simply watch. He goes on: “for contemplation which should be finished in itself, without casting beams upon society, assuredly divinity knoweth it not.”
detailsBody: The story Bacon retells survives in Cicero’s Tusculan Disputations, Book V, which cites Heraclides Ponticus. There, Pythagoras tells Leon, prince of the Phliasii, that the spectators at the games, who seek neither glory nor profit, are “by far the best,” and that in life, too, contemplation “greatly exceeds every other pursuit.” Bacon’s retelling names the listener as Hiero instead (Yonge translation ↗).
